summary: Path steering is a mechanism to discover paths to producers of Information-Centric Networking content and steer later Interest messages along a discovered path. It is useful for multipath congestion control and for measurement and management. This experimental specification derives from an earlier published design.

eli5.summary: You find which road leads to a library, then tell later requests to use the same road. This helps balance traffic and measure the roads.

questions: how does path steering help congestion control
subtitle: Discover and reuse specific network paths in Information-Centric Networking.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking protocols allow discovery of different paths to content, but applications lack a way to control which path subsequent requests use, limiting multi-path congestion control and network measurement capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: This specification defines a path label—a data structure containing nexthop identifiers for each hop—that is built by forwarders as content returns to the consumer, then used by consumers to steer subsequent Interest messages along the same discovered path.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now discover multiple paths to content and explicitly choose which path to use for each request, enabling advanced congestion control, accurate network measurement, and better handling of potential cache poisoning.

today: RFC 9531 is an Experimental specification published in March 2024 by the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It provides a mechanism for experimental implementations of CCNx and NDN to support advanced multi-path congestion control and network measurement, and is not part of any Internet Standard.

sections.title: Information-Centric Networking and Path Choices
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) like CCNx and Named Data Networking (NDN) fundamentally differs from IP routing: consumers request named content rather than specifying a destination address. The network naturally supports multi-path topologies where multiple paths may lead to the same content. However, traditional ICN protocols do not let consumers control which path their requests follow.

Path steering solves this by allowing consumers to discover paths to content producers and then explicitly direct later requests along those paths. This is useful for several important scenarios: advanced multi-path congestion control algorithms that require packets to stay on consistent paths; accurate network performance measurement where multiple consecutive packets must follow the same path; and diagnostic functions like ICN Ping and Traceroute that require path control. Additionally, a consumer can use path steering to avoid potentially poisoned content caches on certain paths.
sections.eli5: Instead of the network deciding which way your request goes, you pick the way after you discover it works.

sections.title: How Path Steering Works
sections.content:
Path steering operates in two phases. In the discovery phase, a consumer sends an Interest message (a content request) without specifying a path. As the Interest traverses the network and the Content (Data) message returns, each forwarder appends information about its outgoing interface to a path label in the Data message. The consumer receives the Data message with a complete path label representing the path the Data took from producer to consumer.

In the steering phase, the consumer can reuse this path label by including it in a subsequent Interest message. Each forwarder along the path reads the path label, extracts the nexthop identifier for that hop, and forwards the Interest through the specified outgoing interface. This ensures the Interest follows the same path as the original request. If the path becomes invalid due to interface changes or routing updates, the forwarder can either return an error or fall back to standard routing, depending on flags set by the consumer.
sections.eli5: First try: the network tells you which way it went. Next try: you tell the network to go that same way.

sections.title: The Path Label Structure
sections.content:
Path labels are encoded as TLV (Type-Length-Value) fields in both CCNx and NDN packets. The specification uses a polynomial encoding with fixed-size bit arrays: each intermediate forwarder gets 12 bits to encode its nexthop identifier, allowing up to 4095 different outgoing interfaces per forwarder. An 8-bit index field tracks which nexthop is currently active.

The path label bitmap accommodates long network paths: even a 24-hop path fits in 36 bytes. This compact representation minimizes overhead while allowing practical networks to be represented. Forwarders increment the index when adding a nexthop to a Data message and decrement it when reading from an Interest message, making the computation at each hop minimal compared to other forwarding operations.
sections.eli5: Each router writes down its door number as the message passes; you read those door numbers to find your way back.

sections.title: Modes and Error Handling
sections.content:
Path labels support three operating modes: DISCOVERY_MODE for discovering new paths, FALLBACK_MODE for graceful handling of stale paths (forwarders use standard routing if the specified path is invalid), and STRICT_MODE for applications requiring exact paths (forwarders return an error if the path is invalid).

When an Interest with an invalid path label arrives at a forwarder in STRICT_MODE, the forwarder returns an InterestReturn (NACK) message with code T_RETURN_INVALID_PATH_LABEL, which also carries the current path label. This allows the consumer to identify exactly which path labels have become stale. Aggregation of multiple Interests at a forwarder is handled normally unless explicitly prevented by unique name suffixes in the Interest.
sections.eli5: You can say 'be strict' (fail if the way is blocked) or 'be flexible' (take a different way if needed).

sections.title: Security Challenges and Mitigations
sections.content:
A malicious consumer could attempt to brute-force valid nexthop labels by sending many Interests with systematically modified path labels. To mitigate this, ICN forwarders are recommended to periodically update nexthop labels (at least every few minutes). With 12-bit labels, brute-forcing requires testing roughly 2048 values per hop on average, an expensive operation when combined with frequent label updates.

The specification also addresses cache poisoning attacks where an attacker might try to populate forwarder caches with false content. Path steering makes traditional on-path cache poisoning possible but does not significantly increase the vulnerability beyond what already exists in ICN protocols. A more sophisticated attack would require computing which off-path paths might be accessible, a complexity comparable to breadth-first search combined with the label-guessing challenge. Forwarders can implement additional defenses like rate limiting on path steering Interests and heuristics to detect systematic label scanning.
sections.eli5: Someone could guess door numbers to steer you to a poisoned cache, but forwarders change the door numbers often, and too many wrong guesses get you rate-limited.

sections.title: Optional Cryptographic Protection
sections.content:
For applications requiring stronger security, path labels can be encrypted hop-by-hop using symmetric keys. Each forwarder receives a Data message with an encrypted path label from the downstream forwarder, decrypts it with its own symmetric key, appends its own nexthop label in cleartext, and re-encrypts the path label with its symmetric key before sending upstream.

When an Interest arrives, the reverse process occurs: each forwarder reads the cleartext nexthop for that hop, decrypts the rest of the path label, and forwards the Interest. This approach prevents consumers from analyzing or modifying the complete path label, eliminating brute-force attack vectors. The encryption adds computational cost comparable to MACsec or IPsec, and implementations may choose to encrypt only at administrative domain boundaries rather than at every hop.
sections.eli5: Scramble the door numbers so only authorized routers can read them and no one can guess them.
